why_this_tool: Next.js puts routing, server rendering, server-side data access, auth checks and end-to-end testing hooks in one codebase, so every subtopic of this lesson can be practised in a single project on a laptop.
alternatives: React Router in framework mode (formerly Remix) is built around web-standard loaders and actions with less caching machinery; a Vite single-page React app is simpler but has no server rendering or server-side data access and needs a separate backend; SvelteKit gives the same full-stack shape with a different component model; Astro suits content-heavy sites with small interactive islands rather than app-like screens.

setup.do: Install a current Node.js LTS release, then create a new Next.js project with create-next-app using the Playwright example, and start the dev server.
setup.done_when: The dev server prints a local address and the starter page loads in your browser.
setup.why: One scaffold gives you the App Router, TypeScript and a working test runner, so later steps add to it instead of rewiring it.

setup.do: Install Tailwind CSS and its peer dependencies into the project.
setup.done_when: The Tailwind packages appear in the project dependencies and the config files exist.
setup.why: Customer screens are judged on polish, and utility classes are the fastest way to style components without leaving the component file.

setup.do: Configure the Tailwind content paths and add the Tailwind directives to the global stylesheet imported by the root layout.
setup.done_when: A utility class added to the home page visibly changes its styling after a refresh.
setup.why: Tailwind only generates classes for files it is told to scan, so a wrong path gives an unstyled page with no error.

steps.do: Write an async Server Component page that fetches a list from a public JSON API with fetch and renders it.
steps.done_when: The list renders in the browser and the browser network tab shows no request to the JSON API.
steps.why: This is the default way data reaches the screen in the App Router: the component awaits data on the server and ships HTML. It is the first run that everything else builds on.

steps.do: Create a Client Component with the use client directive that takes props and holds state, such as a filter box or a like button, and place it on the page.
steps.done_when: Clicking or typing in the component updates the screen without a page reload.

source.title: Getting Started: Server and Client Components | Next.js

steps.why: Components, props and state are the React core model, and in Next.js state and event handlers only work in components marked as client.

steps.do: Write the page so the Server Component fetches the data and passes it as props to the Client Component, then try passing a non-serializable value to see the failure.
steps.done_when: The Client Component renders server-fetched data, and you have seen the error raised for a value that cannot cross the boundary.

steps.why: The server and client boundary is where most App Router bugs come from. Seeing what can and cannot cross it makes the rule concrete.

steps.do: Start PostgreSQL in a local container, then load rows from it inside a Server Component through an ORM or database client.
steps.done_when: Rows you inserted into the local database appear on the page, and the connection string is absent from the browser sources.
steps.why: Customer applications read from the customer's own data, and querying on the server keeps credentials and query logic out of the browser bundle.

steps.do: Create a deliberately slow data component, wrap it in a Suspense boundary with a skeleton fallback, and add a loading file for the route.
steps.done_when: The page shell and skeleton appear immediately and the slow section fills in a few seconds later without a full reload.
steps.why: AI-backed screens often wait on slow calls. Streaming lets the page shell show at once while the slow part arrives later.

steps.do: Compare the client fetching patterns in the guide against your server-fetched page and write down which one each of your screens needs.
steps.done_when: You have a short note that maps each screen in your app to one pattern with a one-line reason.
steps.why: Not every screen should fetch on the server: polling, live updates and user-driven refetching belong on the client. Choosing on purpose avoids duplicated fetch logic.

steps.do: Configure the TanStack Query provider, write a form that mutates a database row through a Server Action, and coordinate the server and client caches after the mutation.
steps.done_when: Submitting the form changes the row in PostgreSQL and the list on screen shows the new value without a manual refresh.

verified.section_found: Coordinate server and client caches after mutations

steps.why: A mutation that saves but leaves stale data on screen is the most visible bug in a customer demo. This is where you learn to keep both caches in agreement.

steps.do: Write sign-up and login forms backed by a stateless session: generate a secret key, encrypt the session, and set it in a cookie with the recommended options.
steps.done_when: After login the browser holds an encrypted HTTP-only session cookie, and after logout it is gone.
steps.why: Building the session by hand once shows what an auth library such as Auth.js does for you, and what to check when a customer security review asks.

steps.do: Create a data access layer that verifies the session before every query, and call it from your pages, Server Actions and route handlers.
steps.done_when: A signed-out request to a protected page or action is redirected or rejected, and a signed-in user sees only their own rows.
steps.why: Authorization must sit next to the data, not only in a redirect, because Server Actions and route handlers can be reached directly. One layer keeps the check consistent.

steps.do: Write a Playwright end-to-end test that logs in, submits the form and checks the updated list, then run it with the CI settings the guide describes.
steps.done_when: The test suite passes in headless mode from a clean checkout with a single command.
steps.why: UI tests are what let you change a customer screen the day before a demo with confidence. Running them the way CI does makes the result reproducible.

steps.do: Configure a deployment ID in the Next config, build the app twice with different IDs, and run the two builds side by side on different local ports as a stand-in for a preview and a live deployment.
steps.done_when: Both builds serve on their own port, and you can find the differing deployment ID in the requests each one makes.
steps.why: Preview and rolling deployments mean two versions are live at once. The deployment ID is how Next.js keeps a browser from mixing assets of different builds. A hosted preview platform is not needed to see this.

steps.do: Read the reference for exposing the testing API in a production build, enable it for a test-only build, then build and start the app in production mode against local PostgreSQL and run the Playwright suite against it.
steps.done_when: The full end-to-end suite passes against the production build served by next start, with the option switched off again for the real release build.
steps.why: The dev server hides caching, minification and prerendering behaviour, so the final check must run against the same kind of build a customer receives.
